deep.reconstruction:
There is no mathematical derivation on this page. It holds four philosophical or programmatic notes from Hilbert's notebook section 'Allgemein Mathem. Philosophisches'.

(1) Lines 1-10 finish a sentence begun at the bottom of the page transcribed as the NEXT page (107): 'Hymne auf den Kreis! ... Wie grade der hohe Reiz der Mathematik darin besteht ohne alle Instrumente | wie sie der Astronom, Physiker, Chemiker gebraucht ...'. The previous page ends '...für seine Untersuchung bloss', which does not connect to this page. So the physical page order and the folio numbering differ from the reading order. The sentence reads: the high charm of mathematics is that, without the instruments of the astronomer, physicist or chemist, without material or technical prior knowledge, and without the source studies of the historian or philologist, one trains one's acumen solely on concepts accessible to everyone (number and circle). In these everyday things, which everyone can imagine but habitually passes by, one sees a significant part of 'that force which holds together the innermost'. This last phrase alludes to Goethe's Faust I, 'was die Welt im Innersten zusammenhält'.

(2) Significance of mathematics (written 'der Wissenschaften') for all sciences, skills and arts. For the practising jurist, a legal decision is like a mathematical problem. Kant took mathematics as his starting point. The reproach of dryness applies in this respect to every science.

(3) Difference between art and science. In science the personal, individual works become outdated quickly while the thought remains eternal. In art it is exactly the reverse, because there form and the formal are the main thing, whereas in science the substance and thought are.

(4) After a struck-out start 'Die Geometrie', a bibliographic note: the analogy of the theory of ideals with the theory of chemical compounds, citing Kummer, Crelle (J. reine angew. Math.) vol. 35, p. 360. This is Kummer's 1847 memoir 'Über die Zerlegung der aus Wurzeln der Einheit gebildeten complexen Zahlen in ihre Primfactoren' (Crelle 35, pp. 327-367). Near its end Kummer compares:
- ideal prime factors to chemical elements or radicals that cannot be isolated (e.g. fluorine, then not yet isolated);
- actual complex numbers to chemical compounds;
- divisibility tests to chemical reagents.

No computation is performed. The illustrative checkable item below is mine, not Hilbert's.

deep.surprise_reason: This is philosophical note-taking plus a reference to Kummer's well-known chemical analogy for ideal numbers. Hilbert as author of the Zahlbericht was thoroughly familiar with Kummer's work. The art/science remark and the 'Hymne auf den Kreis' are mildly interesting for his intellectual biography but contain no new mathematics.
